raw_text:
The subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed to preserve the mortality benefit of ICD therapy while avoiding intravascular and intracardiac leads. Landmark trials established ICDs for primary prevention in ischemic and nonischemic cardiomyopathy [1,2], but transvenous systems expose patients to pneumothorax, venous obstruction, endocarditis, lead fracture, and extraction risk [3,4]. The S-ICD moves the generator to the left lateral thorax and the coil to a parasternal subcutaneous course, using far-field sensing and high-energy shocks without chronic vascular access [5]. Its key trade-off is intentional: no chronic bradycardia pacing, cardiac resynchronization therapy, or monomorphic ventricular tachycardia antitachycardia pacing (ATP).

Early clinical development showed feasibility and high induced and spontaneous ventricular fibrillation conversion. The pivotal IDE study met prespecified safety and efficacy end points in patients with standard ICD indications but no pacing requirement [6]. The EFFORTLESS registry then demonstrated reproducibility in broader international practice [7], and pooled IDE/EFFORTLESS data showed high final shock efficacy, absence of endovascular lead failure, and declining inappropriate shock and complication rates with experience and programming [8]. A multicenter case-control study and the START study further supported broadly comparable clinical performance and rhythm discrimination relative to transvenous ICDs [9,10].

The strongest comparative evidence comes from PRAETORIAN, designed specifically to test S-ICD versus transvenous ICD in patients without pacing indications [11]. In the randomized trial, the S-ICD was noninferior for the composite of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [12]. Secondary analyses clarified the trade-off: transvenous systems retained the advantage of ATP for many ventricular tachycardia episodes [13], whereas S-ICD therapy reduced lead-related complications and systemic infection but had more pocket-related issues [14]. UNTOUCHED extended these findings to contemporary primary-prevention patients with low ejection fraction, showing low inappropriate shock rates with high-rate detection zones, conditional discrimination, and modern filtering [15].

Real-world postapproval data are important because early S-ICD cohorts were relatively young and less comorbid. The US Post-Approval Study enrolled a more diverse population, including patients with renal disease and heart failure [16]. At 1 year, spontaneous ventricular arrhythmias were effectively treated and mortality reflected background comorbidity rather than device failure [17]. Long-term EFFORTLESS and 5-year postapproval follow-up showed durable shock efficacy, few pacing conversions, very low electrode failure, and acceptable complication-free survival [18,19].

Appropriate patient selection remains central. The ideal S-ICD recipient has an ICD indication, reasonable life expectancy, and no current or anticipated need for bradycardia pacing, CRT, or frequent ATP-responsive monomorphic VT. The device is particularly attractive in young patients, inherited arrhythmia syndromes, difficult venous access, prior device infection, hemodialysis, and congenital anatomy in which venous leads are undesirable. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy experience supports feasibility, but screening during posture or exercise may be useful when T-wave oversensing risk is suspected [20]. Conversely, patients with symptomatic bradycardia, high-grade atrioventricular block, wide anticipated pacing needs, CRT indication, or recurrent slow monomorphic VT generally remain better served by transvenous or newer extravascular pacing-capable strategies.

Implant technique has evolved. Preimplant electrocardiographic vector screening reduces sensing failure; posteroanterior and lateral imaging, reflected in the PRAETORIAN score, helps identify suboptimal generator or lead position associated with higher defibrillation thresholds [21]. Although many operators historically performed defibrillation testing, registry data suggest practice variation and the need to balance procedural risk against confirmation of system efficacy [22]. Procedural refinements include the two-incision approach [23], broader validation of two- versus three-incision techniques [24], intermuscular generator placement to improve cosmesis and stability [25], and learning-curve effects that emphasize training and standardization [26].

Current guideline recommendations endorse S-ICD use when ICD therapy is indicated and pacing is not required [29]. Remaining limitations include inappropriate shocks from oversensing, larger generator size, discomfort or cosmetic concerns, need for high-energy shocks, and absent ATP. Nevertheless, contemporary programming, SMART filtering, improved implantation technique, and long-term registry data have narrowed early performance concerns. Future systems that combine an S-ICD with a communicating leadless pacemaker may mitigate the principal limitation—lack of pacing—while preserving an extravascular defibrillator platform [30]. Overall, the S-ICD is no longer a niche device; it is an evidence-based alternative to the transvenous ICD for carefully selected patients in whom lead avoidance is clinically valuable [27,28].
